1.topic: Specialised cells, tissues and the microscope
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. recall the parts of plant and animal cells and their work;
2. explain how specialised cells are suited to their jobs;
3. arrange cells, tissues, organs and systems in order of size;
4. calculate magnification from a drawing.

## Materials

Microscopes with prepared slides (blood smear, onion skin), charts of a root hair cell, red blood cell, nerve cell and muscle cell, rulers, drawing paper.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: a danfo driver, a mechanic and a conductor all work on one bus, but each does a different job. Is the same true for cells in your body? Take two answers.

## Development

1. Quick recall of the cell: membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, plus wall, large vacuole and chloroplasts in plants.
2. Specialised cells have a shape that fits their job. Red blood cells are disc-shaped and carry oxygen; root hair cells have long thin extensions to take in water from soil; nerve cells are long to carry messages; muscle cells can shorten to cause movement.
3. Levels of organisation: cells of the same kind make a tissue; different tissues make an organ; organs working together make a system. Example: muscle cells, muscle tissue, the heart, the circulatory system.
4. Introduce magnification: magnification = size of the image ÷ actual size. Work an example: a drawing 30 mm long of a cell that is really 0.1 mm gives 30 ÷ 0.1 = ×300.
5. Rearrange the formula to find the actual size: actual size = image size ÷ magnification.

## Class activity

Learners study the prepared slide, make a drawing of one cell and measure its width with a ruler, then calculate the actual size using the microscope's magnification.

## Evaluation

1. Why are red blood cells shaped like discs?
2. Put in order: organ, cell, system, tissue.
3. A drawing is 24 mm wide and the magnification is ×120. What is the actual width?

## Assignment

Draw three specialised cells and write under each how its shape helps it do its job. Submit on the app.

reading.title: Cells at work
reading.content:
# Cells at work

## Cells that do special jobs

In the last class we studied the general plant and animal cell. In a real body, however, cells are not all the same. Different cells are **specialised**, which means they have a shape and contents that suit the job they do.

| Cell | Special feature | How it helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Red blood cell | Disc shape, no nucleus | Gives more room to carry oxygen and squeezes through tiny blood vessels |
| Root hair cell | A long thin extension | Gives a large surface to absorb water and mineral salts from the soil |
| Nerve cell | Very long with branches | Carries messages quickly across the body |
| Muscle cell | Can get shorter | Pulls on bones to move the body |

## From cell to system

Cells of one kind joined together form a **tissue**. Muscle tissue is made of muscle cells. Different tissues join to form an **organ**: the heart is made of muscle tissue, blood and nerve tissue. Organs that work together form a **system**: the heart, blood and blood vessels form the circulatory system.

The order from smallest to largest is: **cell → tissue → organ → system → organism**.

## Using a microscope and magnification

A microscope makes small things look bigger. We can calculate how many times bigger a drawing is than the real cell:

**Magnification = size of image ÷ actual size**

**Worked example 1.** A learner draws an onion cell 30 mm long. The real cell is 0.1 mm long.

Magnification = 30 ÷ 0.1 = ×300.

**Worked example 2.** A drawing of a cheek cell is 45 mm wide, and the magnification is ×150. What is the real width?

Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 45 ÷ 150 = 0.3 mm.

Always use the same units for both measurements, and give the answer with its unit.

## Remember

All cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus (red blood cells lose theirs when mature). A plant cell also has a cell wall, a large vacuole and, in green parts, chloroplasts.

2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. state the work of the respiratory, digestive and circulatory systems;
2. trace air through the respiratory system and food through the digestive system;
3. describe how blood moves oxygen and digested food round the body.

## Materials

Charts of the three systems, a model of the lungs (a bottle with balloons), a stethoscope if available, a bicycle pump, a clock for pulse counting.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask learners to run on the spot for one minute. Then ask what changed: breathing, heartbeat, warm skin. Tell them these changes come from three systems working together.

## Development

1. Respiratory system: air enters through the nose, passes the windpipe (trachea), bronchi and into the lungs, where oxygen goes into the blood and carbon dioxide leaves. Use the bottle model: pulling down the rubber sheet makes the balloon inflate.
2. Digestive system: food passes through the mouth, gullet, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The mouth chews and saliva starts to break down starch; the stomach churns food with acid; the small intestine absorbs digested food into the blood; the large intestine absorbs water.
3. Circulatory system: the heart pumps blood round the body in blood vessels. Blood carries oxygen from the lungs and digested food from the small intestine to every cell, and carries carbon dioxide back to the lungs.
4. Measure the pulse at the wrist for 30 seconds at rest and after exercise, and discuss why it changes.
5. Link the three systems: the lungs supply oxygen, digestion supplies food, the blood delivers both so that cells can release energy.

## Class activity

Learners trace and label the path of a mouthful of rice and a breath of air on an outline body, and record their pulse at rest and after exercise.

## Evaluation

1. Where does digested food enter the blood?
2. What does the blood carry from the lungs to the cells?
3. Why do we breathe faster when we run?

## Assignment

Draw the path of food through the body and write one job for each organ on the path. Submit on the app.

reading.title: Three systems that keep us going
reading.content:
# Three systems that keep us going

## The respiratory system: getting oxygen

When you breathe in, air goes through your nose or mouth, down the windpipe (**trachea**), through two tubes called **bronchi** and into the **lungs**. In the lungs there are millions of tiny air sacs. Oxygen passes from the air sacs into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes out of the blood into the air sacs and leaves when you breathe out.

Muscles between the ribs and the **diaphragm** below the lungs move to make you breathe in and out.

## The digestive system: getting food ready

Digestion breaks big pieces of food into small soluble ones that the blood can carry.

1. **Mouth:** teeth chew the food, and saliva begins to digest starch.
2. **Gullet:** a tube that pushes the food down to the stomach.
3. **Stomach:** muscles churn the food and acid and juices break it down.
4. **Small intestine:** digestion finishes here and the digested food passes into the blood.
5. **Large intestine:** water is taken out and the rest leaves the body as faeces.

## The circulatory system: delivery service

The **heart** is a muscle that pumps blood through **blood vessels** to every part of the body. Blood carries:

- oxygen from the lungs to the cells;
- digested food from the small intestine to the cells;
- carbon dioxide from the cells back to the lungs.

The **pulse** you feel at your wrist is the beat of the heart pushing blood along an artery. At rest an adult's pulse is about 70 beats per minute. After exercise it is faster because the cells need more oxygen.

**Worked example.** A learner counts 36 beats in 30 seconds. The pulse in one minute is 36 × 2 = 72 beats per minute.

## Working together

Without the lungs there is no oxygen, without digestion there is no usable food, and without the blood neither would reach the cells.

3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. name the parts of a flower and say what each does;
2. describe pollination and fertilisation;
3. say how seeds are spread;
4. state what photosynthesis is, what it needs and what it makes.

## Materials

Fresh hibiscus or pawpaw flowers, a hand lens, a blade, a potted plant, a leaf that has been in the dark and one in the sun, a chart of the flower.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Hold up a hibiscus flower. Ask: where does a mango come from? Lead to the idea that every fruit starts as a flower.

## Development

1. Parts of a flower: petals attract insects; sepals protect the bud; stamens (anther and filament) make pollen; the carpel or pistil (stigma, style, ovary) holds the ovules. Dissect a hibiscus and name the parts.
2. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma, by insects or wind. Fertilisation happens when the pollen's male cell joins the female cell in the ovule.
3. After fertilisation the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
4. Seeds are spread by wind (silk cotton, tridax), animals (spear grass sticks on clothes), water (coconut) and explosion (flame of the forest pods).
5. Photosynthesis: plants make food in leaves. Carbon dioxide + water, in sunlight and with chlorophyll, gives glucose and oxygen. Write the word equation and discuss why plants are the base of food chains.
6. Show the test for starch with iodine on a leaf that has been in light (blue-black) and one kept in the dark (stays brown).

## Class activity

Groups dissect a flower, stick the parts on paper, and label each with its job.

## Evaluation

1. What is pollination?
2. What does a plant need to carry out photosynthesis?
3. Why is a leaf kept in the dark unable to make starch?

## Assignment

Collect two fruits at home and write which part of the flower each came from and how its seeds might be spread.

reading.title: From flower to fruit, and how plants make food
reading.content:
# From flower to fruit, and how plants make food

## Parts of a flower

A flower is the part of the plant that makes seeds.

- **Petals** are often bright, and they attract insects.
- **Sepals** are small leaf-like parts that protect the flower when it is a bud.
- **Stamens** are the male parts. The **anther** makes the yellow dust called pollen.
- **Carpel** is the female part. It has a **stigma** (sticky top that catches pollen), a **style** and an **ovary** that holds the **ovules**.

## Pollination and fertilisation

**Pollination** is when pollen is carried from an anther to a stigma. Insects such as bees do this when they visit flowers for nectar. Wind carries the pollen of grasses like maize.

After pollination, a tube grows down the style, and the male cell from the pollen joins an ovule. This is **fertilisation**. The ovule becomes a **seed** and the ovary becomes the **fruit**.

## Spreading seeds

Seeds must be spread so the young plants do not crowd the parent. Wind carries light seeds, such as those of the silk cotton tree. Animals carry seeds that stick to fur or are eaten, such as those of the guava. Water carries coconuts. Pods of flame of the forest burst open and throw seeds out.

## Photosynthesis

Plants make their own food in the green parts of the leaf by **photosynthesis**.

carbon dioxide + water, in sunlight and with chlorophyll → glucose + oxygen

- Carbon dioxide comes from the air through tiny pores in the leaf.
- Water comes from the soil through the roots.
- **Chlorophyll** is the green substance in chloroplasts that traps sunlight energy.
- The **glucose** is used for energy or changed to starch for storage. The oxygen is released into the air.

**Worked example.** A student covers part of a leaf with black paper for three days. She tests the leaf with iodine. The covered part stays brown but the part in the light turns blue-black, because only the part in the light made starch.

Photosynthesis feeds the plant, and the oxygen it releases is what animals breathe.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. list the components of soil;
2. compare sandy, clayey and loamy soil;
3. do a simple calculation of soil composition;
4. explain why soil matters to the farmer.

## Materials

Samples of sandy, clayey and loamy soil, a tall transparent jar, water, funnels with cotton wool, measuring cylinders, a stopwatch, a kitchen scale.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Show three handfuls of soil from different places. Ask learners to rub each between the fingers and describe how it feels. Record the words gritty, sticky and smooth.

## Development

1. Soil is made of mineral particles (from broken rock), humus (decayed plants and animals), water, air and living organisms such as earthworms and bacteria.
2. Soil types by particle size: sand (large, gritty), silt (medium, smooth) and clay (very small, sticky). Loam is a mixture of all three with plenty of humus.
3. Experiment 1: shake a soil sample in a jar of water, let it settle, and observe the layers: sand at the bottom, then silt, then clay, with humus floating.
4. Experiment 2: pour 100 ml of water through 100 g of each soil in a funnel and time how fast it drains and how much is collected. Sandy soil drains fast; clay holds water.
5. Compare in a table: drainage, water held, air spaces, suitable crops (groundnut and cassava on sandy soil; rice on clay; most crops on loam).
6. Importance of soil: it anchors plants, supplies water and mineral salts, and is home to many organisms. Discuss soil erosion and how to prevent it.

## Class activity

Groups carry out the jar test and funnel test and record results in a table.

## Evaluation

1. Which soil type is best for most crops, and why?
2. Why does rice grow well on clay soil?
3. Name three things found in soil besides rock particles.

## Assignment

Collect a small sample of soil near your house, describe how it feels and decide whether it is more sandy, clayey or loamy.

# Looking closely at soil

## What soil is made of

Soil is not just crushed rock. A handful of garden soil contains:

- **mineral particles** from rocks broken down by weather over thousands of years;
- **humus**, the dark material from dead plants and animals that have rotted;
- **water** held between the particles;
- **air** in the spaces between the particles;
- **living things**, such as earthworms, termites, fungi and bacteria.

## Types of soil

| Soil | Particle size | Feel | Drainage | Water held |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sandy | Large | Gritty | Fast | Little |
| Silty | Medium | Smooth, like flour | Medium | Medium |
| Clayey | Very small | Sticky when wet | Slow | Much, can waterlog |
| Loam | Mixture of all three plus humus | Crumbly | Good | Good |

**Loam** is the best soil for most crops because it holds water and air and has plenty of humus. Sandy soil suits groundnut and cassava, which like good drainage. Rice is often grown on clay soil that holds water.

## Doing a soil test

Put a spoonful of soil in a jar of water, shake well and leave for a day. The heaviest particles, the sand, settle first at the bottom, then silt, then clay. Humus floats on top.

**Worked example.** A 200 g sample is separated and found to have 120 g sand, 50 g silt and 30 g clay.

- Percentage of sand = 120 ÷ 200 × 100 = 60%.
- Percentage of silt = 50 ÷ 200 × 100 = 25%.
- Percentage of clay = 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%.
- The three percentages add up to 100%, so the work checks. The soil is mostly sand, so it will drain quickly.

## Why soil matters

Soil holds the roots of a plant firmly. It supplies water and mineral salts for growth. It is home to organisms that recycle dead plants into humus. But heavy rain can wash away the top layer, which is called **erosion**. Farmers prevent it by planting cover crops, making ridges across a slope and keeping a layer of mulch.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain why living things are classified;
2. group animals into vertebrates and invertebrates and name the five vertebrate groups;
3. tell an insect from a spider;
4. group plants and say why fungi are not plants.

## Materials

Specimens or pictures of tilapia, toad, lizard, hen, goat, grasshopper, spider, earthworm, a maize plant, a bean plant, a mushroom, and a fern.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Give each group a bag of ten pictures and ask them to sort the pictures in any way they like. Let two groups explain how they sorted. Point out that scientists also sort but use agreed rules.

## Development

1. Classification is putting living things into groups by their shared features. It helps us study the huge number of living things and name them in a way everyone understands.
2. Two big groups of animals: vertebrates (with a backbone) and invertebrates (without).
3. Vertebrates: fish (gills, scales, fins, live in water), amphibians (moist skin, young in water, adults on land, e.g. toad), reptiles (dry scaly skin, lay eggs on land, e.g. lizard), birds (feathers, wings, lay hard-shelled eggs), mammals (hair or fur, feed young on milk).
4. Invertebrates: insects (6 legs, 3 body parts, antennae), arachnids (8 legs, 2 body parts, no antennae, e.g. spider), worms (soft bodies without legs) and molluscs (e.g. snail).
5. Plants: flowering plants (maize, bean) and non-flowering plants (ferns, mosses). Maize has narrow leaves with parallel veins (monocot); bean has broad leaves with branching veins (dicot).
6. Fungi, like mushrooms, are not plants: they have no chlorophyll and get food from rotting material. Bacteria are tiny single-celled organisms.

## Class activity

Groups make a classification chart on cardboard with the pictures stuck in the correct boxes.

## Evaluation

1. Name the five groups of vertebrates.
2. How do you know a spider is not an insect?
3. Why is a mushroom not a plant?

reading.content:
# Sorting out living things

## Why classify?

There are millions of kinds of living things. To study them we put those with shared features into groups. This is **classification**. It is like arranging goods in Balogun market by type so that you can find what you want.

## Animals

Animals are first divided into:

- **Vertebrates**, which have a backbone;
- **Invertebrates**, which do not.

### The five groups of vertebrates

| Group | Features | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fish | Gills, scales and fins; live in water | Tilapia, catfish |
| Amphibians | Moist skin; young live in water, adults on land | Toad, frog |
| Reptiles | Dry scaly skin; lay eggs on land | Lizard, crocodile |
| Birds | Feathers and wings; lay hard-shelled eggs | Hen, pigeon |
| Mammals | Hair or fur; feed their young on milk | Goat, bat, human |

### Invertebrates

- **Insects:** six legs, three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen) and one pair of antennae. Many have wings. Examples: grasshopper, housefly, bee.
- **Arachnids:** eight legs and two body parts. No antennae and no wings. Examples: spider, scorpion.
- **Worms:** soft bodies without legs, such as earthworms.
- **Molluscs:** soft bodies, often with a shell, such as snails.

## Plants

Flowering plants make seeds in flowers. Some have narrow leaves with parallel veins (like maize), and some have broad leaves with branching veins (like beans). Non-flowering plants, such as ferns and mosses, reproduce using spores.

## Fungi and bacteria

A mushroom looks like a plant but it has no chlorophyll, so it cannot make its own food. It feeds on dead material. Fungi are a group on their own. Bacteria are tiny living things made of a single cell, some helpful, such as the ones used to make yoghurt, and some harmful.

**Worked example.** A creature has eight legs, two body parts and no wings. It is an arachnid, not an insect.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. name the forms of energy and give an example of each;
2. say which energy changes happen in everyday devices;

## Materials

A torch, a small solar panel with a bulb, a hand-cranked radio or dynamo, a bicycle, a candle, a bell, a pencil sharpener, charts of power stations.

2. Forms: heat (thermal), light, sound, electrical, mechanical (kinetic energy of moving things and potential energy stored by position or stretching), chemical (in food, fuel and batteries) and nuclear (inside atoms).
3. Energy changes: a torch turns chemical energy to electrical, then to light and heat; a generator turns kinetic energy to electrical; a solar panel turns light to electrical; a loudspeaker turns electrical to sound.
4. Sources: renewable ones are not used up (the sun, wind, flowing water, biomass); non-renewable ones are finite (crude oil, coal, natural gas). Nigeria's examples: Kainji and Jebba dams (water), Niger Delta oil, solar for rural villages.
5. Law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Some always turns into unwanted heat.
6. Draw the energy change for a bicycle dynamo lamp and for a candle.

## Class activity

Learners complete an energy chain for five devices and sort a set of cards into renewable and non-renewable sources.

reading.content:
# Where does energy come from, and where does it go?

## What is energy?

Energy is the ability to make things move, heat up, light up or change. It is measured in **joules (J)**. A person, a generator and a fire all use or give energy.

## Forms of energy

- **Heat (thermal) energy:** from a fire or a cooker.
- **Light energy:** from the sun or a lamp.
- **Sound energy:** from a drum or a radio.
- **Electrical energy:** from the NEPA line, a battery or a generator.
- **Mechanical energy:** of moving things (**kinetic**) and of stored position, like water in a dam or a stretched spring (**potential**).
- **Chemical energy:** stored in food, firewood, petrol and batteries.
- **Nuclear energy:** stored inside atoms and released in nuclear power stations and in the sun.

## Energy changes

Energy often changes from one form to another.

- A torch: chemical → electrical → light (and some heat).
- A solar panel: light → electrical.
- A generator: chemical (petrol) → kinetic → electrical.
- A radio: electrical → sound.
- A person running: chemical (food) → kinetic and heat.

## Conservation of energy

Energy is never created or destroyed. It is only changed from one form to another. Not all the energy ends up as the form we want: when a bulb gives light, much of the energy escapes as heat. The total energy stays the same.

## Sources of energy

**Renewable** sources do not run out: the sun, wind, flowing water and biomass (firewood, if trees are replanted). **Non-renewable** sources are used up and take millions of years to form: crude oil, coal and natural gas.

Nigeria gets electricity from dams such as Kainji and Jebba on the River Niger (water), and from gas-burning power stations (natural gas). Many villages now use solar panels.

**Worked example.** In a hydroelectric dam, water high up has potential energy. It falls and gains kinetic energy, and turns a turbine that drives a generator, which gives electrical energy: potential → kinetic → electrical.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe conduction, convection and radiation;
2. name the method of heat transfer in everyday situations;
3. explain how a vacuum flask and light-coloured clothes reduce heat transfer.

## Materials

A metal spoon and a wooden spoon, hot water, a candle with wax and pins, a beaker with potassium permanganate crystal, a heat source, a lamp, a black and a white tin with thermometers, a vacuum flask.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: why do we stir soup with a wooden spoon and not a metal one? Collect ideas about the spoon handle getting hot and lead into conduction.

## Development

1. Conduction: heat passes through a solid from particle to particle without the material moving. Metals are good conductors; wood, plastic and air are poor conductors (insulators). Fix pins with wax along a metal rod and heat one end; the pins drop in order.
2. Convection: in liquids and gases, hotter parts expand, become less dense and rise, while cooler, denser parts sink, making a current. Drop a crystal of potassium permanganate in water and heat below it to see the current.
3. Radiation: heat travels as waves and needs no material; it crosses empty space, as the sun's heat reaches the earth. Dark, dull surfaces absorb and give out more radiation; shiny, light surfaces reflect it.
4. Compare black and white tins in the sun with thermometers inside, and record the temperature every 3 minutes.
5. Vacuum flask: a vacuum between double glass walls stops conduction and convection; the silvered walls reflect radiation; the stopper stops heat leaving by convection through the top.
6. Everyday examples: a pot with a plastic handle, a sea breeze, white-painted houses and light clothes in hot weather, warm air rising above a fire.

## Class activity

In groups, learners label the method of heat transfer in ten pictures, and predict the results of the black and white tin test.

## Evaluation

1. Why do cooking pots have plastic handles?
2. Why does smoke from a fire go upward?
3. How does the heat of the sun reach the earth through space?

## Assignment

Make a list of five things at home that use heat transfer and say which method each uses. Submit on the app.

reading.title: How heat travels
reading.content:
# How heat travels

Heat always flows from a hot place to a cooler one. It can travel in three ways.

## Conduction

In a solid, the particles vibrate. When one end of a metal rod is heated, those particles vibrate more and pass the energy to the particles next to them, and so on along the rod. The material itself does not move. This is **conduction**.

Metals such as copper and iron are **good conductors**. Wood, plastic, cloth and air are **poor conductors** (insulators). That is why a cooking pot is made of metal but has a plastic or wooden handle.

## Convection

In liquids and gases, heat travels by **convection**. When water at the bottom of a pot is heated, it expands, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler water, which is denser, sinks to take its place. A circle of moving water, a **convection current**, forms and spreads the heat.

Convection explains why smoke goes up, why a sea breeze blows in the afternoon (warm air over the land rises and cool air from the sea moves in), and why an air conditioner is fixed high on the wall.

## Radiation

The heat from the sun reaches us through space, where there is no air. It travels as waves, and this is **radiation**. Radiation needs no material to travel through.

Dark, dull surfaces **absorb** radiation well and also give it out well. Light, shiny surfaces **reflect** it. That is why people wear white or light clothes in hot weather, and why houses in hot towns like Kano are often painted white.

## The vacuum flask

A vacuum flask keeps tea hot for hours because it stops all three:

- the **vacuum** between the double glass walls stops conduction and convection;
- the walls are **silvered** to reflect radiation;
- the **stopper** is a poor conductor and closes the top.

## Worked example

You sit near a fire. The heat reaches your hands in three ways: by radiation across the air, by convection as warm air rises, and by conduction if you touch a hot metal poker. Which one do you feel most when standing to the side? Radiation, because hot air rises upward and not sideways.

9.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain that sound comes from vibrating objects;
2. say that sound needs a material to travel and compare its speed in solids, liquids and gases;
3. calculate distance from the speed of sound and the time taken;
4. describe echoes, pitch, loudness and noise dangers.

## Materials

A ruler, a talking drum or tuning fork, a rubber band, a bell jar if available (or a diagram), a loudspeaker, a stopwatch, a tape measure, a chart of the decibel scale.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Hold a ruler on a desk and twang it. Ask what the learners can see and hear. Place a hand on the throat while humming. Tell them that sound always comes from something vibrating.

## Development

1. Sound is produced by vibrating objects, such as a drum skin, a guitar string, the air in a flute, or the vocal cords.
2. Sound travels as waves through a medium (solid, liquid or gas) and cannot travel through a vacuum. Show the diagram of a bell ringing in a bell jar with the air removed.
3. Speed of sound: about 340 m/s in air, 1,500 m/s in water and over 5,000 m/s in steel. It travels fastest in solids.
4. Calculation: distance = speed × time. Thunder is heard 3 s after lightning, so the storm is 340 × 3 = 1,020 m away. Echo: sound travels to a wall and back, so the wall is half the total distance.
5. Pitch is how high or low a sound is (faster vibration gives higher pitch); loudness depends on the size of the vibration, measured in decibels (dB).
6. Uses: music, communication, sonar for finding fish, ultrasound scans for babies in the womb. Dangers: noise from loud generators and loudspeakers can damage hearing; above about 85 dB for long periods is harmful. Ways to reduce it: ear protection, distance, quieter machines.

## Class activity

Learners take the class outdoors to measure the time for an echo off a school wall and calculate how far away the wall is.

## Evaluation

1. What must be present for sound to travel?
2. A drum is heard 2 s after it is seen being hit. How far away is it? (Take the speed of sound as 340 m/s.)
3. Name two ways to protect your hearing from loud noise.

## Assignment

Find out from a relative which noises in your area (generator, loudspeaker, market) are loud, and suggest two ways to reduce them. Submit on the app.

reading.title: Sound and its journey
reading.content:
# Sound and its journey

## Making sound

Every sound is made by something that **vibrates**, which means it moves quickly backwards and forwards. A drum makes sound when the skin vibrates. A guitar gives sound when its strings vibrate. When you speak, your vocal cords vibrate.

## How sound travels

The vibrating object pushes on the air next to it, and this movement passes from particle to particle, as a wave, until it reaches your ear. Sound needs a **medium** (a solid, liquid or gas) to travel through. In a vacuum, where there are no particles, there is no sound. That is why astronauts talk by radio in space.

Sound travels faster when the particles are closer together.

| Medium | Speed of sound |
| --- | --- |
| Air | about 340 m/s |
| Water | about 1,500 m/s |
| Steel | over 5,000 m/s |

## Calculating distance

Distance = speed × time

**Worked example 1.** You hear thunder 3 seconds after the lightning flash. How far away was the lightning? Distance = 340 × 3 = 1,020 m.

**Worked example 2 (echo).** A boy shouts in front of a cliff and hears the echo 2 seconds later. The sound goes to the cliff and back, so the total distance is 340 × 2 = 680 m. The cliff is half of this: 680 ÷ 2 = 340 m away.

An **echo** is sound that has bounced off a hard surface.

## Pitch and loudness

- **Pitch** is how high or low a note sounds. A fast vibration gives a high pitch, as in a whistle; a slow vibration gives a low pitch, as in a big bass drum.
- **Loudness** depends on how big the vibration is. It is measured in **decibels (dB)**. A whisper is about 30 dB, a conversation about 60 dB and a loud generator or loudspeaker 90 dB or more.

## Uses and dangers

Sound is used for music, speech and warning signals. Ships use sonar to find fish, and doctors use ultrasound to look at a baby in the womb.

Long exposure to loud sounds, such as a generator beside the house or a loudspeaker at a party, can damage hearing for life. We can protect ourselves by keeping away from loud noises, using ear protection and keeping the volume low.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. state the law of reflection and use it to find angles;
2. describe the image formed by a plane mirror;
3. explain refraction with everyday examples;
4. name uses of convex and concave lenses and mirrors.

## Materials

A plane mirror, a protractor, a ray box or torch with a slit, a glass of water with a pencil, a convex lens (magnifying glass), a concave and a convex mirror (or a shiny spoon), paper.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Put a pencil in a glass of water and ask learners to look from the side. Ask: why does the pencil look bent? Record their ideas and say that light changes direction when it moves between substances.

## Development

1. Reflection: light bounces off a smooth surface. The normal is an imaginary line at 90° to the surface. The law: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
2. Work: if a ray makes an angle of incidence of 35°, the angle of reflection is 35° and the angle between the incident and reflected rays is 70°. If the ray makes 20° with the surface, the angle of incidence is 90 − 20 = 70°.
3. A plane mirror image is the same size as the object, the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted (left and right swapped).
4. Refraction: light bends when it passes from one transparent material into another because its speed changes. It bends towards the normal when it enters water or glass from air. This makes a pool look shallower than it is and a straw look bent.
5. Lenses: a convex lens is thicker in the middle and brings rays together (magnifying glass, camera, projector, eye). A concave lens is thinner in the middle and spreads rays out (used for short-sighted eyes).
6. Curved mirrors: concave mirrors collect light (torch and car headlamp reflectors, shaving mirrors); convex mirrors give a wide view (driving mirrors, shop security mirrors).

## Class activity

Learners draw ray diagrams for a plane mirror, a glass of water and a convex lens with a magnifying glass, and measure angles with a protractor.

## Evaluation

1. A ray hits a mirror at an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of reflection?
2. Why does a river look shallower than it is?
3. Which kind of lens is a magnifying glass?

## Assignment

reading.content:
# Bouncing and bending light

## Reflection

When light hits a smooth, shiny surface such as a mirror, it bounces off. This is **reflection**. Scientists measure angles from the **normal**, an imaginary line drawn at 90° to the surface.

**The law of reflection:** the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

**Worked example 1.** A ray of light hits a plane mirror and makes an angle of incidence of 35°. The angle of reflection is also 35°, so the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 35° + 35° = 70°.

**Worked example 2.** A ray makes 20° with the surface of the mirror. The normal is 90° from the surface, so the angle of incidence is 90° − 20° = 70°, and so the angle of reflection is 70°.

### The image in a plane mirror

The image you see in a flat mirror is the same size as you, as far behind the mirror as you stand in front, and the left and right are swapped (this is called lateral inversion).

## Refraction

When light passes from one transparent material into another, it changes speed and **bends**. This is **refraction**.

- When light goes from air into water or glass, it bends **towards** the normal.
- Because of this a pencil in a glass of water looks bent, and a river looks shallower than it really is.

## Lenses

A **convex lens** is thicker in the middle. It brings rays of light together. Magnifying glasses, cameras, projectors and the lens in your eye are convex.

A **concave lens** is thinner in the middle and spreads light out. It is used in spectacles for short-sighted people.

## Curved mirrors

- A **concave mirror** gathers light. It is used behind a torch bulb or a car headlamp to give a strong beam, and as a shaving mirror to give a large image.
- A **convex mirror** curves outwards and shows a wide area. It is used as a driving mirror and in shops so that the owner can see all corners.
